claim: Alzheimer's Disease (AD) is the leading cause of senile dementia with over 44 million affected persons and an economic burden of over $600 billion.
source: Alzheimer's Disease (AD) is the leading cause of senile dementia with over 44 million affected persons and an economic burden of over $600 billion (Mayeux and Stern, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mayeux and Stern, 2012.

claim: 60–90% of AD brains have evidence of cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA), cerebral small vessel disease and microvascular degeneration.
source: In addition to AD's neuropathological hallmarks of amyloid plaques consisting of deposited Aβ peptides and neurofibrillary tangles consisting of hyperphosphorylated tau proteins, 60–90% of AD brains have evidence of cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA), cerebral small vessel disease and microvascular degeneration (Attems and Jellinger, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Attems and Jellinger, 2014.

claim: Apolipoprotein E is the principal lipid carrier within the central nervous system (CNS).
source: Apolipoprotein (apo) E, which in the brain is secreted primarily from astrocytes, is the principal lipid carrier within the central nervous system (CNS) and, in humans, exists as three isoforms, namely APOE2, APOE3, and APOE4 (Lane-Donovan and Herz, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lane-Donovan and Herz, 2017.

claim: ApoE in the brain is secreted primarily from astrocytes.
source: Apolipoprotein (apo) E, which in the brain is secreted primarily from astrocytes, is the principal lipid carrier within the central nervous system (CNS) and, in humans, exists as three isoforms, namely APOE2, APOE3, and APOE4 (Lane-Donovan and Herz, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lane-Donovan and Herz, 2017.

claim: In humans, apoE exists as three isoforms: APOE2, APOE3, and APOE4.
source: Apolipoprotein (apo) E, which in the brain is secreted primarily from astrocytes, is the principal lipid carrier within the central nervous system (CNS) and, in humans, exists as three isoforms, namely APOE2, APOE3, and APOE4 (Lane-Donovan and Herz, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lane-Donovan and Herz, 2017.

claim: ApoE4 is detrimental, apoE3 is neutral, and apoE2 is protective with respect to Aβ metabolism.
source: ApoE has well-established effects on Aβ metabolism with apoE4 being detrimental, apoE3 neutral and apoE2 protective.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: ApoE is hypothesized to contribute to cerebrovascular dysfunction.
source: ApoE is also hypothesized to contribute to cerebrovascular dysfunction (Zlokovic, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zlokovic, 2013.

claim: The major routes by which Aβ is cleared from the brain involve the cerebrovasculature.
source: As the major routes by which Aβ is cleared from the brain involve the cerebrovasculature (Ueno et al., 2014), understanding the vascular contributions to dementia is of great interest (Snyder, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ueno et al., 2014.

claim: Cardiovascular risk factors including type two diabetes mellitus (T2DM), hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, obesity and stroke increase AD risk.
source: Cardiovascular risk factors including type two diabetes mellitus (T2DM), hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, obesity and stroke increase AD risk (Duron and Hanon, 2008), yet the mechanisms by which cardiovascular health impacts brain function remain poorly understood.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Duron and Hanon, 2008.

claim: Epidemiological studies suggest that AD risk may be attenuated by high levels of circulating high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C).
source: Interestingly, epidemiological studies suggest that AD risk may be attenuated by high levels of circulating high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C), which is also highly associated with reduced cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk (Zuliani et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zuliani et al., 2010.

claim: Levels of apoA-I positively correlate with Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and Cognitive Ability Screening Instrument (CASI) scores.
source: Specifically, levels of apoA-I, the major HDL-associated protein, positively correlate with Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and Cognitive Ability Screening Instrument (CASI) scores (Merched et al., 2000)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Merched et al., 2000.

claim: High serum HDL-C levels (>55 mg/dl) in cognitively normal elderly individuals is associated with significantly reduced risk (HR 0.4) of AD even after adjusting for APOE genotype and vascular risk factors.
source: and high serum HDL-C levels (>55 mg/dl) in cognitively normal elderly individuals is associated with significantly reduced risk (HR 0.4) of AD even after adjusting for APOE genotype and vascular risk factors including obesity and T2DM (Reitz et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Reitz et al., 2010.

claim: In symptomatic AD patients, plasma apoA-I levels negatively correlate with hippocampal and whole brain volume as well as mean entorhinal cortical thickness.
source: In symptomatic AD patients, plasma apoA-I levels negatively correlate with hippocampal and whole brain volume as well as mean entorhinal cortical thickness (Hye et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hye et al., 2014.

claim: Decreased levels of serum apoA-I can discriminate AD from non-demented age-matched control subjects.
source: and decreased levels of serum apoA-I can discriminate AD from non-demented age-matched control subjects (Shih et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Shih et al., 2014.

claim: HDL and apoE have several potent vasoprotective functions including reducing inflammation, increasing vascular tone through promoting endothelial nitric oxide (NO) synthase activity, and suppressing vascular adhesion molecule expression.
source: As HDL and apoE have several potent vasoprotective functions including reducing inflammation, increasing vascular tone through promoting endothelial nitric oxide (NO) synthase activity, and suppressing vascular adhesion molecule expression (Stukas et al., 2014b; Sacre et al., 2003)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Stukas et al., 2014b and Sacre et al., 2003.

claim: The major circulating lipoprotein in mice is HDL whereas low-density lipoprotein (LDL) is the major circulating lipoprotein in humans.
source: However, lipoprotein metabolism in mice and humans are substantially different, as the major circulating lipoprotein in mice is HDL whereas low-density lipoprotein (LDL), which increases CVD risk, is the major circulating lipoprotein in humans (Yin et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yin et al., 2012.

claim: Bioengineered bipartite vessels were fabricated by sequentially seeding primary human myofibroblasts and ECs isolated from umbilical cords into a tubular woven scaffold consisting of polyglycolic acid (PGA), polycaprolactone (PCL) and polylactate (PLA), measuring 15 mm long and 2 mm in diameter.
source: Bipartite bioengineered vessels were fabricated by sequentially seeding primary human myofibroblasts and ECs isolated from umbilical cords into a tubular woven scaffold consisting of polyglycolic acid (PGA), polycaprolactone (PCL) and polylactate (PLA), measuring 15 mm long and 2 mm in diameter (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methods used to fabricate the vessels, supported by reference to Figure 1.

claim: After 4 weeks in culture, Haematoxylin-Eosin staining demonstrated the formation of a dense and homogenous tissue on the luminal side of the scaffold.
source: After 4 weeks in culture, Haematoxylin-Eosin staining demonstrated the formation of a dense and homogenous tissue on the luminal side of the scaffold (Figure 2a).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological staining data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The bioengineered tissue was composed of cells and extracellular matrix, as demonstrated by the presence of collagen by Picrosirius staining.
source: The tissue was composed of cells and extracellular matrix, as demonstrated by the presence of collagen by Picrosirius staining (Figure 2b)
evidence: The claim is supported by Picrosirius staining data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Immunohistochemical staining confirmed collagen IV and laminin in the extracellular matrix of bioengineered vessels.
source: and confirmed by immunohistochemical detection of collagen IV and laminin in the extracellular matrix (Figure 2c–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 2c-d.

claim: Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated multiple layers of α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA) positive cells on the inner side of the scaffold and a monolayer of CD31 positive ECs lining the bioengineered vascular lumen.
source: Immunohistochemical staining also demonstrated multiple layers of α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA) positive cells on the inner side of the scaffold and a monolayer of CD31 positive ECs lining the bioengineered vascular lumen (Figure 2e–f).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 2e-f.

claim: Evans blue penetrated into tissue prepared without EC, whereas it was excluded two weeks after EC seeding, demonstrating a functionally tight endothelial barrier.
source: As expected, Evans blue penetrated into tissue prepared without EC, whereas it was excluded two weeks after EC seeding, demonstrating a functionally tight endothelial barrier (Figure 2g).
evidence: The claim is supported by Evans blue exclusion assay data shown in Figure 2g.

claim: Bioengineered vessels could be fabricated with brain derived SMC (hBSMC) and microvascular cortical EC (hBMEC).
source: In addition to cord cells, bioengineered vessels could also be fabricated with brain derived SMC (hBSMC) and microvascular cortical EC (hBMEC).
evidence: The claim describes experimental observations about vessel fabrication.

claim: Brain-derived and cord-derived primary human cells form similar structures in bioengineered vessels.
source: Immunohistological staining confirmed that brain-derived and cord-derived primary human cells form similar structures in bioengineered vessels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistological staining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Brain-derived and cord-derived cells function similarly with respect to tissue Aβ accumulation and transport.
source: and function similarly with respect to tissue Aβ accumulation and transport (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b–e).
evidence: The claim is supported by functional assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b-e.

claim: Both ELISA and 6E10 immunostaining confirmed dose-dependent retention of Aβ40 and Aβ42 within the bioengineered vascular wall 48 hr after injection.
source: Both ELISA (Figure 3a,b) and 6E10 immunostaining (Figure 3c–f) confirmed dose-dependent retention of Aβ40 and Aβ42 within the bioengineered vascular wall 48 hr after injection (white), which could be distinguished from autofluorescence by residual scaffold material (shaded in blue).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA and immunostaining data shown in Figure 3a-f.

claim: Thioflavin-S staining confirmed dose-dependent fibrillization in the bioengineered vessels.
source: As Aβ fibrillization within the vessel wall is an important feature of CAA, we also stained vessels using Thioflavin-S (Thio-S), and confirmed dose-dependent fibrillization in the bioengineered vessels (Figure 3e–f).
evidence: The claim is supported by Thioflavin-S staining data shown in Figure 3e-f.

claim: Both ELISA quantification and 6E10 immunostaining revealed Aβ deposition by 2 hr after injection, after which Aβ levels remained stable for up to 72 hr.
source: Both ELISA quantification and 6E10 immunostaining revealed Aβ deposition by 2 hr after injection, after which Aβ levels remained stable for up to 72 hr (Figure 3g–h).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA and immunostaining data shown in Figure 3g-h.

claim: Quantification of beta-sheet formation in bioengineered tissue lysates with Thioflavin-T revealed increasing signal over time.
source: Interestingly, quantification of beta-sheet formation in bioengineered tissue lysates with Thioflavin-T also revealed increasing signal over time (Figure 3i–j), biochemically confirming increased Aβ fibrillization into beta-sheet structures within bioengineered vessels after seeding of Aβ monomers.
evidence: The claim is supported by Thioflavin-T quantification data shown in Figure 3i-j.

claim: Confocal microscopy of immunofluorescent staining against amyloid fibrils using the OC antibody demonstrated that fibrillary Aβ accumulates outside of the cells.
source: Specifically, confocal microscopy of immunofluorescent staining against amyloid fibrils using the OC antibody demonstrated that fibrillary Aβ accumulates outside of the cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a–b)
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a-b.

claim: 6E10 staining revealed both extracellular accumulation and intracellular vesicular deposition of Aβ.
source: whereas 6E10 staining revealed both extracellular accumulation and intracellular vesicular deposition (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b–f).
evidence: The claim is supported by 6E10 staining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b-f.

claim: ELISA quantification revealed that both Aβ40 and Aβ42 were transported at a slower rate in bioengineered vessels, whereas Aβ freely diffused across scaffold-only controls.
source: ELISA quantification revealed that both Aβ40 and Aβ42 were transported at a slower rate in bioengineered vessels, whereas Aβ freely diffused across scaffold-only controls (Figure 3k–l).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA quantification data shown in Figure 3k-l.

claim: Neither apoE isoform significantly altered the rate of recovery of Aβ into the circulation medium over 4 hr.
source: Although neither apoE isoform significantly altered the rate of recovery of Aβ into the circulation medium over 4 hr (Figure 4a–b)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4a-b.

claim: A significant and selective decrease of the amount of Aβ42 deposited into the bioengineered tissue after 24 hr was observed with apoE2 co-injection.
source: we observed a significant and selective decrease of the amount of Aβ42 deposited into the bioengineered tissue after 24 hr with apoE2 co-injection (Figure 4c–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4c-d.

claim: Over 4 hr, the levels of Aβ42 and Aβ42 recovered in the circulation medium were slightly increased in the presence of HDL, but this did not reach significance.
source: Over 4 hr, the levels of Aβ42 and Aβ42 recovered in the circulation medium were slightly increased in the presence of HDL, but this did not reach significance (Figure 4e,f).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4e-f.

claim: After 24 hr, a strong trend toward decreased tissue levels of accumulated Aβ40 and significantly lower accumulated Aβ42 was observed in the presence of HDL.
source: After 24 hr, we observed a strong trend toward decreased tissue levels of accumulated Aβ40 and significantly lower accumulated Aβ42 in the presence of HDL (Figure 4g–h).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4g-h.

claim: The combination of anteluminal apoE2 and circulating luminal HDL led to significantly increased Aβ40 and Aβ42 transport over 4 hr compared to either Aβ alone or Aβ with apoE2 or HDL alone.
source: Importantly, the combination of anteluminal apoE2 and circulating luminal HDL led to significantly increased Aβ40 and Aβ42 transport over 4 hr compared to either Aβ alone or Aβ with apoE2 or HDL alone (Figure 5a–b).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5a-b.

claim: The levels of Aβ42 accumulated in the tissue were significantly reduced by apoE2, HDL, and the combination of both apoE2 and HDL.
source: however, the levels of accumulated Aβ42 were significantly reduced by apoE2, HDL, and the combination of both apoE2 and HDL (Figure 5d).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The combination of anteluminal apoE4 and circulating luminal HDL significantly increased both Aβ40 and Aβ42 transport over 4 hr compared to either Aβ alone or Aβ with apoE4.
source: Interestingly, the combination of anteluminal apoE4 and circulating luminal HDL significantly increased both Aβ40 and Aβ42 transport over 4 hr compared to either Aβ alone or Aβ with apoE4 (Figure 5e–f)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5e-f.

claim: The level of Aβ42 accumulated in the tissue at 24 hr was significantly lower in the presence of both apoE4 and HDL compared to Aβ42 alone or Aβ42 and apoE4.
source: and concomitantly the level of Aβ42 accumulated in the tissue at 24 hr was significantly lower in the presence of both apoE4 and HDL compared to Aβ42 alone or Aβ42 and apoE4 (Figure 5h).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5h.

claim: Tripartite bioengineered vessels are composed of EC lining the lumen, several layers of SMC, and a layer of astrocytes in the antelumen.
source: Tripartite bioengineered vessels are therefore composed of EC lining the lumen, several layers of SMC, and a layer of astrocytes in the antelumen as confirmed by immunofluorescent staining against CD31, α-SMC actin, and GFAP, respectively (Figure 6a–c).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescent staining data shown in Figure 6a-c.

claim: Higher magnification images revealed GFAP positive protrusions penetrating into the tissue, suggestive of astrocyte endfeet.
source: Interestingly, higher magnification images revealed GFAP positive protrusions penetrating into the tissue (Figure 6d), suggestive of astrocyte endfeet.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: Peripherally-derived ECs (HUVEC), when cultured in the presence of astrocytes and under flow conditions, expressed high level of the tight-junction proteins ZO-1 and ZO-2.
source: Importantly, we observed that peripherally-derived ECs (HUVEC), when cultured in the presence of astrocytes and under flow conditions, expressed high level of the tight-junction proteins ZO-1 and ZO-2 (Figure 6e–f)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescent staining data shown in Figure 6e-f.

claim: Peripherally-derived ECs (HUVEC), when cultured in the presence of astrocytes and under flow conditions, expressed the blood brain barrier (BBB) tight junction protein Claudin 5.
source: as well as the blood brain barrier (BBB) tight junction protein Claudin 5 (Figure 6g)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescent staining data shown in Figure 6g.

claim: Peripherally-derived ECs (HUVEC), when cultured in the presence of astrocytes and under flow conditions, expressed the specific BBB transporter Glut-1.
source: and the specific BBB transporter Glut-1 (Figure 6h), demonstrating that the EC phenotype of a HUVEC is reprogrammed to become brain-like in the presence of astrocytes.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescent staining data shown in Figure 6h.

claim: The EC phenotype of a HUVEC is reprogrammed to become brain-like in the presence of astrocytes.
source: demonstrating that the EC phenotype of a HUVEC is reprogrammed to become brain-like in the presence of astrocytes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the expression of BBB-specific markers in HUVECs cultured with astrocytes.

claim: Evans blue was excluded in both tripartite and bipartite vessels.
source: As expected, Evans blue was excluded in both tripartite and bipartite vessels (Figure 6j).
evidence: The claim is supported by Evans blue exclusion assay data shown in Figure 6j.

claim: Tripartite tissues demonstrated less extravasation of both 4 kDa and 40 kDa FITC-dextran than bipartite tissues, although these were not significantly different from each other.
source: Tripartite tissues demonstrated less extravasation of both 4 kDa and 40 kDa than bipartite tissues, although these were not significantly different from each other, whereas, as expected, both tissues are significantly less permeable than unseeded scaffold (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by permeability assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: A significant increase in NO production was observed after treatment with acetylcholine or HDL, whereas in the presence of L-NAME, the conversion was blocked.
source: A significant increase was observed after both treatments, whereas, in the presence of the specific NO synthase inhibitor L-NG-nitroarginine methyl ester (L-NAME), the conversion was blocked (Figure 6k).
evidence: The claim is supported by NO production assay data shown in Figure 6k.

claim: GW3965 significantly stimulated the secretion of native apoE in the tripartite vessels.
source: ELISA quantification demonstrated that GW3965 significantly stimulated the secretion of native apoE in the tripartite vessels (Figure 6l).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA quantification data shown in Figure 6l.

claim: Neither GW3965 alone nor HDL alone modified the rate of Aβ40 or Aβ42 transport through tripartite vessels over 4 hr.
source: Consistent with our observations in bipartite vessels, neither GW3965 alone nor HDL alone modified the rate of Aβ40 or Aβ42 transport through tripartite vessels over 4 hr (Figure 7a,b).
evidence: The claim is supported by transport assay data shown in Figure 7a-b.

claim: The combination of GW3965 and HDL together resulted in a significantly increased initial rate of Aβ42 transport without affecting Aβ40.
source: However, the combination of GW3965 and HDL together resulted in a significantly increased initial rate of Aβ42 transport without affecting Aβ40 (Figure 7a,b).
evidence: The claim is supported by transport assay data shown in Figure 7a-b.

claim: Neither GW3965, HDL, nor both GW3965 and HDL affected accumulation of Aβ40 or Aβ42 within tripartite tissues after 24 hr.
source: Interestingly, relative to baseline tripartite conditions, neither GW3965, HDL, nor both GW3965 and HDL affected accumulation of Aβ40 or Aβ42 within tripartite tissues after 24 hr (Figure 7c,d)
evidence: The claim is supported by tissue accumulation data shown in Figure 7c-d.

claim: Tripartite tissue lysates had significantly more apoE than bipartite tissue under baseline conditions.
source: Western blotting confirmed that tripartite tissue lysates had significantly more apoE than bipartite tissue under baseline conditions (Figure 7e).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 7e.

claim: Increased Aβ42 but not Aβ40 recovery into circulation medium was observed in tripartite compared to bipartite vessels.
source: We then directly compared Aβ transport and tissue accumulation between bipartite and tripartite vessels and observed increased Aβ42 but not Aβ40 recovery into circulation medium in tripartite compared to bipartite vessels (Figure 7f,g).
evidence: The claim is supported by transport assay data shown in Figure 7f-g.

claim: Aβ42 levels were significantly lower and Aβ40 levels showed a trend toward lower levels in tripartite compared to bipartite vessels.
source: With respect to tissue accumulation, Aβ42 levels were significantly lower and Aβ40 levels showed a trend toward lower levels in tripartite compared to bipartite vessels (Figure 7h,i).
evidence: The claim is supported by tissue accumulation data shown in Figure 7h-i.

claim: Significantly slower transport of Aβ40 and Aβ42 fibrils compared to monomers was observed in tripartite vessels.
source: To test this, we compared Aβ transport and accumulation by injecting either monomeric or pre-aggregated Aβ40 or Aβ42 on the anteluminal side of tripartite vessels, and observed significantly slower transport of Aβ40 and Aβ42 fibrils compared to monomers (Figure 8a–b).
evidence: The claim is supported by transport assay data shown in Figure 8a-b.

claim: Tissue accumulation was significantly increased after injection of fibrils compared to monomers.
source: Furthermore, tissue accumulation was significantly increased after injection of fibrils compared to monomers (Figure 8a–b).
evidence: The claim is supported by tissue accumulation data shown in Figure 8a-b.

claim: No significant difference in Aβ accumulation was observed between bipartite and tripartite tissues 24 hr after injection of pre-formed Aβ40 and Aβ42 fibrils.
source: To test whether native astrocyte-secreted apoE might reduce aggregation of pre-formed Aβ40 and Aβ42 fibrils (Castellano et al., 2011), we quantified Aβ levels in bipartite and tripartite tissues 24 hr after injection of pre-formed Aβ40 and Aβ42 fibrils and observed no significant difference in Aβ accumulation (Figure 8c–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by tissue accumulation data shown in Figure 8c-d.

claim: Astrocyte-derived apoE specifically facilitates transport of soluble Aβ from the brain.
source: Together, these data suggest that astrocyte-derived apoE specifically facilitates transport of soluble Aβ from the brain.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that apoE affects soluble but not fibrillar Aβ transport.

claim: Aβ40 is the predominant species found in human CAA.
source: These data are consistent with the observation that Aβ40 is the predominant species found in human CAA (Yamada, 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yamada, 2015.

claim: Aβ42 is reported to be essential for CAA development in mice.
source: even though Aβ42 is reported to be essential for CAA development in mice (McGowan et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to McGowan et al., 2005.

claim: Recombinant apoE2 promotes more Aβ42 clearance than recombinant apoE4.
source: Our results are also consistent with the hypothesized effects of apoE isoform on vascular function, as we demonstrate that recombinant apoE2 promotes more Aβ42 clearance than recombinant apoE4.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing apoE2 and apoE4 effects.

claim: Lipoproteins including brain (apoE) and circulating (high-density lipoprotein, HDL) synergize to facilitate Aβ transport across bioengineered human cerebral vessels.
source: We show that lipoproteins including brain (apoE) and circulating (high-density lipoprotein, HDL) synergize to facilitate Aβ transport across bioengineered human cerebral vessels.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing synergistic effects of apoE and HDL.

claim: These lipoproteins facilitate Aβ42 transport more efficiently than Aβ40.
source: These lipoproteins facilitate Aβ42 transport more efficiently than Aβ40, consistent with Aβ40 being the primary species that accumulates in CAA.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing differential effects on Aβ40 vs Aβ42.

claim: ApoE4 is less effective than apoE2 in promoting Aβ transport.
source: Moreover, apoE4 is less effective than apoE2 in promoting Aβ transport, also consistent with the well-established role of apoE4 in Aβ deposition in AD.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing apoE2 and apoE4 effects.

claim: This study presents the first functional 3-dimensional model of CAA in bioengineered human vessels.
source: Here we present a notable advance in vascular tissue engineering by generating the first functional 3-dimensioinal model of CAA in bioengineered human vessels.
evidence: The claim describes the novelty of the experimental model developed in this study.

claim: The generation of a functional, 3D cerebrovascular model using primary human ECs, SMCs and astrocytes represents a major advance in the bioengineering field.
source: Importantly, the generation of a functional, 3D cerebrovascular model using primary human ECs, SMCs and astrocytes represents a major advance in the bioengineering field.
evidence: The claim describes the significance of the experimental model developed in this study.
